def: The dot product of two vectors gives a scalar related to the angle between them; the cross product gives a new vector perpendicular to both, used for areas.
points: Dot product: a.b = |a||b| cos(theta), a scalar number.
Dot product in components: a.b = a1b1 + a2b2 + a3b3.
Cross product: a x b = |a||b| sin(theta) n-hat, a vector perpendicular to both a and b.
Cross product is computed using the 3x3 determinant with i, j, k in the first row.
Dot product is used for angles and projections; cross product is used for areas and perpendicular directions.
a.b = 0 means vectors are perpendicular; a x b = 0 means vectors are parallel.

diagram.draw: Draw two vectors a and b starting from the same point, with the angle theta marked between them. For cross product, draw a third vector perpendicular to the plane of a and b using the right-hand rule.

tip: Set up the determinant carefully with i, j, k on top row and a, b components below — sign errors in the j term are common.

def: The scalar triple product [a b c] is the determinant formed from the components of three vectors; it equals zero exactly when the three vectors are coplanar.
points: Write the components of a, b, c as three rows of a 3x3 determinant.
Evaluate the determinant to get the scalar triple product value.
The value also equals the volume of the parallelepiped formed by the three vectors.
If the value is zero, the three vectors lie in the same plane (coplanar).
If nonzero, the vectors are not coplanar and form a genuine 3D parallelepiped.
Order of vectors in the determinant can change the sign but not whether it is zero.
formula: [a b c] = determinant of a,b,c components; coplanar if [a b c]=0

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Write a, b, c as rows"] --> B["Compute 3x3 determinant"]
  B --> C{"Value is zero"}
  C -->|"yes"| D["Vectors coplanar"]
  C -->|"no"| E["Not coplanar, forms volume"]

tip: Expand the determinant along the first row consistently; keep signs (+,-,+) in order to avoid errors.

def: The section formula gives the position vector of a point dividing a line segment in a given ratio; collinearity of points is checked by showing one vector is a scalar multiple of another.
points: For point P dividing AB internally in ratio m:n, position vector = (m*b + n*a)/(m+n).
For external division, use (m*b - n*a)/(m-n).
Midpoint is the special case m=n=1: (a+b)/2.
Three points A, B, C are collinear if vector AB = k * vector AC for some scalar k.
Alternatively check if vector AB x vector AC = 0 (cross product zero means parallel, hence collinear).
Always express points as position vectors from a common origin before applying the formula.

diagram.draw: Draw a line segment from point A to point B. Mark point P between them dividing AB in ratio m:n, with m on the A side and n on the B side.

tip: Clearly state which end the ratio m:n starts from (A to B) — reversing it gives a wrong point.

def: The angle between two vectors is found from their dot product; the projection of one vector on another gives its component along that direction.
points: cos(theta) = (a.b) / (|a||b|) gives the angle between vectors a and b.
Compute a.b and the magnitudes |a|, |b| separately first.
Projection of a on b = (a.b)/|b|, a scalar length.
Vector projection of a on b = [(a.b)/|b|^2] * b, a full vector in the direction of b.
If a.b = 0, vectors are perpendicular (theta = 90 degrees).
Always simplify the final angle using inverse cosine if an exact value is not standard.
formula: cos(theta)=(a.b)/(|a||b|)     Projection of a on b = (a.b)/|b|

diagram.draw: Draw vector b along a horizontal line. Draw vector a starting from the same point at an angle. Drop a perpendicular from the tip of a onto line b, marking the projected length on b.

example: a=(1,0,0), b=(1,1,0): a.b=1, |a|=1, |b|=sqrt2. cos(theta)=1/sqrt2, so theta=45 degrees.
tip: Do not confuse scalar projection (a number) with vector projection (a vector) — state which one is asked.

def: The cross product magnitude gives the area of the parallelogram formed by two vectors; half of that gives the area of the triangle formed by them.
points: For vectors a and b as adjacent sides, parallelogram area = |a x b|.
Triangle area (with a and b as two sides from a common vertex) = (1/2)|a x b|.
First compute a x b using the determinant method.
Then find its magnitude using sqrt of sum of squares of components.
For a triangle given by three points, use two side vectors from one vertex.
Units of area are always squared units.
formula: Parallelogram area = |a x b|     Triangle area = (1/2)|a x b|

diagram.draw: Draw a parallelogram with two adjacent sides as vectors a and b from the same vertex. Draw the diagonal to show the triangle is exactly half the parallelogram.

example: a=i+2j+3k, b=3i-2j+k: a x b = 8i+8j-8k, |a x b| = sqrt(64+64+64) = 8sqrt3. Parallelogram area = 8sqrt3, triangle area = 4sqrt3.
tip: Remember the factor of 1/2 for triangle area — a very common point lost by forgetting it.

def: Lines and geometric relations can be expressed in vector form using a position vector and a direction vector, which simplifies solving applied geometry problems.
points: Vector equation of a line through point A with direction b: r = a + t*b, t is a scalar parameter.
Different values of t give different points on the line.
Vector equations can represent motion, forces, or geometric conditions compactly.
To check if a point lies on the line, see if it fits r = a + t*b for some real t.
Vector equations are converted to Cartesian form by equating i, j, k components.
Many geometry proofs (medians, diagonals) become simple algebra using position vectors.
formula: r = a + t*b (vector equation of a line)

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Point A with position vector a"] --> B["Add t times direction vector b"]
  B --> C["Get general point r on line"]

example: Line through (1,0,0) with direction (2,1,1): r = (1,0,0) + t(2,1,1) = (1+2t, t, t).
tip: Always define the parameter (commonly t or lambda) explicitly when writing the vector equation.
